articles.title: Here’s the full text of Jensen Huang’s memo to Nvidia
articles.summary: In the memo Nvidia’s CEO acknowledges having an affair with a suspected Chinese spy.
articles.body: On Sunday, Nvidia announced it was launching an investigation into CEO Jensen Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang, an AI executive and agent of the Chinese government. In addition to the Board of Directors announcing the investigation, Huang sent a memo to Nvidia employees acknowledging the affair. You can read the full text below. > To my colleagues at NVIDIA, > I owe my family and all of you an apology. > I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry. > Throughout my life, my family has given me love and support. They deserve my honesty and loyalty. Instead, I let them down and damaged the life we built together. I take full responsibility for what I did and the hurt I caused, and I accept the criticism that comes with it. > To my wife and family: I love you. I know an apology cannot undo what I have done. I hope our family will heal and that, over time, I can earn back your trust. > To my colleagues at NVIDIA, including those I have worked alongside for decades, and to our board, partners, and shareholders around the world: you deserve better from me. Leading NVIDIA is the privilege of my life. My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust. I have fallen short of that responsibility. I am fully committed to NVIDIA and will work to earn back your confidence. > Regarding the national security concerns raised in news reports, NVIDIA’s Board of Directors has initiated an independent investigation. I support the investigation and will cooperate fully. I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America’s national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American. > My family bears no responsibility for my choices. I do. Please give them privacy. > — Jensen

articles.title: Trump Backs Nvidia CEO After He Admits Affair With Suspected Spy
articles.summary: President Donald Trump called Jensen Huang a “fine person” and said he should stay on as the chief executive officer of Nvidia Corp. after the executive admi...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- President Donald Trump called Jensen Huang a "fine person" and said he should stay on as the chief executive officer of Nvidia Corp. after the executive admitted having an affair with a suspected Chinese spy.

"I have not spoken to him about it," Trump told reporters on Sunday before returning to Washington. "I just know he's a fine person, but you never know what is going on."

Asked whether he should stay on, Trump said, "I think so. Oh yeah, sure."

Nvidia said its board would begin an investigation into whether Huang was a target of a foreign intelligence agency.

Asked if he plans to take Huang on his trip to Asia later this month, Trump said that he doesn't know but would take him along.

"I haven't heard he's done anything wrong," Trump said.

US intelligence officials had told the Trump administration earlier that a woman who had become close to Huang was working for a Chinese spy agency, which recruited her to collect information on him, the New York Times reported Friday. On Sunday, the newspaper reported that Secretary of State Marco Rubio had overseen the production of a secret memo on US concerns.

articles.title: Nvidia CEO’s Affair Admission Counters Past Statements on Ties
articles.summary: For more than a year, Nvidia Corp. minimized the ties that Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang had with Megaspeed, the once-obscure spinoff of a Chinese gam...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- For more than a year, Nvidia Corp. minimized the ties that Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang had with Megaspeed, the once-obscure spinoff of a Chinese gaming enterprise, and a woman named Huang Le who helped set it up.

Both Nvidia and Jensen Huang had characterized Megaspeed as a legitimate, albeit large, buyer of Nvidia's AI chips despite US government concerns that China could be using the Singapore-based firm to gain access to advanced semiconductors. And they'd described reports of Jensen's relationship with Huang Le, who also goes by Alice Huang, as professional in nature.

Just in the past two weeks, despite reports of a close relationship between the two, Jensen defended himself, calling their interactions "completely normal."

Those comments made Jensen Huang's admission that he'd cheated on his wife of more than four decades all the more shocking, contrasting with his and the company's past statements. On Sunday, Nvidia said its board was investigating whether he'd been "the target of a foreign intelligence effort," following reports that US officials suspected Alice Huang was hired by a Chinese spy agency. The revelations have left Jensen Huang's future as the face of the AI infrastructure boom and head of one of the world's most valuable companies hanging in the balance.

Jensen Huang's ties to Alice Huang date as far back as 2024. The New York Times reported in October 2025 that she was mingling with a group of tech executives at a bar in Taipei a year earlier when she bet she could get Jensen to join them. Shortly after Alice Huang reached out, the Times reported, Jensen Huang showed up and took a whiskey shot with the group.

In response to that report, Nvidia spokesman John Rizzo said at the time that the company's "field operations teams often host groups of customers and partners at conferences, and when Jensen is available, may ask him to visit to provide updates on the market."

Nvidia continued to defend its business with Megaspeed, a so-called neocloud that rents out access to computing power for AI workloads, when Bloomberg News reported last December that the US government had been investigating Megaspeed's ownership structure and whether the firm had diverted Nvidia chips to China. Such smuggling would represent a major breach of US curbs aimed at limiting China's AI and military prowess.

articles.title: Is Jensen Huang’s job on the line? Yale’s Jeffrey Sonnenfeld estimates it’s “about a 50-50” | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Nvidia’s board is investigating Jensen Huang over his relationship with a suspected Chinese spy, and Yale’s Jeffrey Sonnenfeld thinks it’s roughly a coin flip whether Huang stays on as CEO.
articles.body:
Nvidia’s board announced Sunday that it’s launching an independent investigation after CEO Jensen Huang told staff he was unfaithful to his wife. But this isn’t a case of just another CEO having an extramarital affair. The romantic interest is Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, whom U.S. officials believe is a Chinese spy who was feeding information back to Beijing. In short, the stakes reach well beyond Nvidia, given how many tech and financial partners depend on its place at the center of the AI economy. “I’m responsible for an entire industry ,” Huang recently told Bloomberg in a sit-down.

A spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in Washington dismissed the allegations in late October as “ groundless smears and slanders ,” and no one has been charged. But U.S. intelligence officials reportedly briefed President Donald Trump about their concerns a year ago, and unnamed senior officials inside the Trump administration told the Times that they doubt Huang could have remained unaware all that time of Alice Huang’s intelligence-gathering role for China. When Trump was first briefed, the Times reported, officials didn’t believe Huang knew, and it isn’t clear whether their assessment has changed. The board, meanwhile, says it sees no sign that national security or company secrets were compromised.

The question is whether Huang can survive this. To think through what could come next, this editor spoke Sunday with famed professor Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, senior associate dean for leadership studies at the Yale School of Management and founder of the Chief Executive Leadership Institute, which has hosted Huang at its CEO summits. Sonnenfeld likes Huang, he said, and he called Huang’s career salvageable but put the odds at “about a 50-50.” He also had a lot more food for thought.

First, the damage. Until now, Huang has been “revered and trusted by everybody in technology,” Sonnenfeld noted. But he called this episode “remarkably poor judgment.” Even if Huang was merely naive, he said, “any employee in Nvidia other than him would be fired over this,” and the recklessness alone would mean “an irretrievable loss of confidence.”

Sonnenfeld suggested that Huang’s saving grace could be what social psychologists call idiosyncrasy credits , if he can prove he was being duped. The term comes from Edwin Hollander, a social psychologist who proposed in a 1958 paper that people earn latitude in a group by showing competence and following its rules. Huang has been earning latitude since he co-founded Nvidia in 1993. But all that goodwill can run out when a screw-up looks self-serving or touches the group’s core norms. Here that group includes Nvidia’s board, its roughly 42,000 employees who are bound by security rules, and, in a looser sense, the U.S. government, given it restricts its exports.

We also talked about precedents, except, as it turns out, there really are none for what’s unfolding right now. Executives who survive personal scandals sometimes pick up where they left off at another company, Sonnenfeld observed. Former HP CEO Mark Hurd is one example. Between 2005 and 2010, he drove HP to the top of the tech industry by revenue, then was pressured to resign after he filed inaccurate expense reports that hid a personal relationship with a contractor. Oracle hired him about a month later. Huang has no equivalent because Nvidia is his company

As for the bench at Nvidia, that doesn’t really exist either. While there is typically a hierarchy inside companies of Nvidia’s scale and importance, Huang has kept things as flat as possible, with about 60 direct reports by his own account. That structure makes it hard to figure out who would succeed him (though his children, both of whom work at Nvidia, are sometimes the subject of succession speculation ). That won’t stop the worldwide guessing game that’s sure to follow. And boards in crisis often reach for a “messianic solution” from outside, Sonnenfeld said, floating former Google CEO Eric Schmidt as one idea.

Nvidia’s role at the center of a massive and complex circular financing web is what makes this particular predicament so tricky and, undoubtedly, terrifying for a wide number of constituents. Nvidia isn’t just the biggest provider of chips driving the AI boom but also largely the bank behind the buildout. In addition to stakes in hundreds of smaller startups, Nvidia has invested in OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI, CoreWeave and Nebius. In August, it also signed preliminary agreements with Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs and KKR aimed at mobilizing more than $500 billion over time, and Huang has said Nvidia could backstop up to a quarter of it. The move was widely interpreted as a way to spread risk. Still, a leadership crisis at the center is how a stumble becomes a collapse.

So what’s Nvidia’s board likely doing right now? Sonnenfeld noted that Huang’s constant, public advocacy for selling advanced chips to China had already made people anxious. Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, whose company Nvidia has backed, had a lot to say about selling chips to China at Davos back in January, likening it to “ selling nuclear weapons to North Korea .”

Now the board’s independent members — meaning everyone but Huang — will have to establish what technology reached China if any, and by what routes, including by better understanding Nvidia’s relationship with Megaspeed. The Singapore cloud company, which grew out of a Chinese gaming business and became Nvidia’s largest buyer in Southeast Asia, bought roughly $2 billion of its chips , the New York Times reported in October 2025, raising broader questions about whether it was helping China circumvent U.S. export restrictions by re-exporting the chips to China or renting them to Chinese customers remotely. (An Nvidia spokesperson told The Hill after the Times report that the allegations were “thoroughly investigated and debunked last year .”)

In the meantime, Huang will keep running the company, Nvidia said Sunday. That’ll be a tall order, even for a CEO who already spends much of his time traveling the world to promote Nvidia. For starters, three House chairmen want a closed-door briefing from Huang on November 18. Nvidia is also reporting its newest earnings on November 17. Sonnenfeld expects that even if Huang keeps the title, he’ll have to hand off some of the day-to-day decision-making.

Only one thing is certain right now. Huang doesn’t own the kind of super-voting stock that would cement his power at Nvidia. Sonnenfeld often argues for dual-class structures that empower founders, and he says Huang’s success without one has been the best counterargument to that case. But if Huang had one, Sonnenfeld continued, removing him would be harder.

This episode may be remembered as a pivotal moment for how the tech industry guards its secrets. Sonnenfeld argues tech has been “way too lax” compared with defense contractors that face clearance regimes. The arrest last month of an OpenAI engineer points to the same problem. He was accused of hiding a recording device behind a TV in an executive conference room, and while OpenAI has said it has no indication that model weights, source code, or customer data were accessed, the case highlights how exposed tech companies are to people who get close.

Huang may well survive the investigation (Sonnenfeld hopes the board clears him of knowingly aiding anyone). The bigger test comes when Nvidia’s employees, customers and partners, and, indirectly, the millions of Americans with Nvidia in their 401(k) plans, have to decide whether an AI economy built largely on the judgment of Huang still makes sense.

articles.title: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman says he does not want his son to have an AI chatbot as his best friend; reveals why children need greater protection from AI
articles.summary: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has expressed reservations about children developing relationships with artificial intelligence chatbots, saying he does not want
articles.body: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has expressed reservations about children developing relationships with artificial intelligence chatbots, saying he does not want his son to have an AI bot as his best friend. He made that particular remark during a US Senate hearing in May 2025. More recently, in an exclusive interview with Vanity Fair, published on October 5, 2026, Altman discussed raising children in a world increasingly shaped by AI and said he had not decided at what age he would allow his own children to use ChatGPT. He also voiced concerns about excessive technology use during childhood and the potential effects of emerging technologies on developing brains. His comments come amid growing concerns among child development experts about AI companions, emotional dependence and children's ability to build meaningful human relationships.Why Sam Altman is cautious about introducing AI to his childrenSpeaking to Vanity Fair, Altman said he had not settled on an appropriate age for his children to start using ChatGPT. He indicated that he was not comfortable introducing the technology to them at their current age.The OpenAI chief also expressed support for limiting children's exposure to technology more broadly. He believes young children should have opportunities to spend time outdoors, play in nature and experience the world beyond screens.Altman raised concerns about children becoming accustomed to touchscreens and short-form videos at an early age. He also pointed to the uncertainty surrounding the effects of emerging technologies on developing brains.He acknowledged that children growing up today would inevitably encounter AI and would need to understand how to use it. However, he questioned whether introducing conversational AI during early childhood was necessary, particularly when its long-term effects on development are still being studied.What Sam Altman said about AI becoming a child's best friendAltman had addressed the question of AI companionship during a US Senate Committee on Commerce, Science and Transportation hearing on May 8, 2025.During the hearing, Senator Bernie Moreno referred to Altman's experience as a new father and asked whether he wanted his child's best friend to be an AI bot. Altman responded directly: "I do not."He subsequently explained that children needed a much higher level of protection when interacting with AI services than adult users. He said OpenAI wanted to give adults considerable freedom in using its products while applying stricter rules and safeguards for younger users.Altman also acknowledged the difficulty of reliably determining whether an online user is a child or an adult. He said that if technology companies could identify users' ages with greater certainty, they could offer adults more flexibility while maintaining tighter restrictions for children.During the same discussion, he raised concerns about people increasingly turning to AI systems for life advice and emotional support. He described the development as relatively new and said it needed to be understood and monitored carefully.Experts are concerned about children forming emotional bonds with AIThe growing popularity of AI companion applications has prompted warnings from child welfare organisations and psychological experts. Unlike conventional search engines or digital assistants, AI companions are designed to maintain conversations, respond to personal information and simulate relationships.This can make interactions feel like conversations with friends, mentors or confidants. However, the responses are generated by AI systems rather than people with genuine emotions or personal experiences.In June 2025, the American Psychological Association (APA) published its health advisory, Artificial Intelligence and Adolescent Well-being. It highlighted concerns about adolescents developing unhealthy relationships with chatbots and warned that young users may be less likely than adults to question the accuracy and intentions of information provided by AI systems.The advisory also warned that adolescents may struggle to distinguish simulated empathy from genuine human understanding. Strong attachments to AI characters could interfere with the development of real-world relationships and social skills.The APA recommended age-appropriate privacy settings, interaction limits, transparency about AI-generated responses and human oversight. It also called for developers to establish clear boundaries around simulated human relationships to prevent AI systems from undermining real-world connections.The organisation acknowledged that AI can support young people through educational and creative activities, including brainstorming, summarising and understanding information. However, it emphasised the need to make children aware of the technology's limitations.Nearly three in four teenagers have used AI companions, study findsResearch published by Common Sense Media on July 16, 2025, highlighted how widely AI companions had spread among teenagers in the United States.Its report, Talk, Trust, and Trade-Offs: How and Why Teens Use AI Companions, surveyed 1,060 US teenagers aged 13 to 17 in April and May 2025. It found that 72% had used AI companions, while 52% said they used them at least a few times a month. Around 33% reported using these platforms for social interaction and relationships.Among teenagers who had used AI companions, 33% said they had chosen to discuss important or serious matters with an AI companion instead of a real person. The survey also found that 24% of AI companion users had shared personal or private information, such as their real name, location or personal secrets, with these platforms.The research also offered a more nuanced picture of teenagers' relationships with AI. Despite widespread adoption, 80% of teenagers who had used AI companions said they spent more time with real-life friends than with AI companions. Additionally, 67% found conversations with AI less satisfying than conversations with their real-life friends.The findings suggest that although AI companions are becoming part of teenagers' social experiences, many young users continue to value human friendships more highly.What UNICEF says about protecting children from AI companionsUNICEF has also highlighted the risks associated with AI systems designed to act as friends or emotional companions.In a July 2025 article published by UNICEF Innocenti, titled The Risky New World of Tech's Friendliest Bots, researchers highlighted concerns about children's growing use of AI companions. The article featured research and an interview with digital innovation specialist Samia Firmino, examining the potential effects of these platforms on young users.It raised concerns about inadequate safety protections, inappropriate chatbot responses and the possibility of children developing unhealthy attachments to artificial companions.UNICEF subsequently updated its Guidance on AI and Children in December 2025. The third version included specific recommendations addressing AI companions and their potential impact on children's rights and well-being.The guidance calls on governments and technology companies to prioritise children's safety, protect their personal information, ensure transparency and establish accountability for AI systems. It also emphasises the importance of designing technology around children's developmental needs and preparing them to use AI responsibly.UNICEF recognises that AI can provide educational opportunities and improve accessibility for children, including those with disabilities. However, it stresses that these benefits must be balanced against the risks associated with children's interactions with increasingly sophisticated AI systems.You use AI every day.
